concepts.name: Pitch
concepts.explanation: How high or low a note sounds, set mainly by its frequency. Doubling the frequency gives the same note an octave higher.
concepts.caveat: Pitch is perceived, not just measured; we hear notes an octave apart as "the same" because of how hearing works.
concepts.question: Why do a man and a woman singing "the same" note often sing an octave apart?

concepts.name: Overtone series
concepts.explanation: Musical tones contain a fundamental plus overtones at whole-number multiples of its frequency; these shape timbre and relate to intervals.
concepts.caveat: The overtone series is often used to "explain" harmony, but culture and learning also shape what sounds consonant.
concepts.question: Which interval appears between the first two overtones above the fundamental?

concepts.name: Interval
concepts.explanation: The distance between two pitches, named by size and quality, such as a major third or perfect fifth.
concepts.caveat: The same interval can have different names depending on spelling (for example augmented fourth versus diminished fifth).
concepts.question: How many semitones are in a perfect fifth?

concepts.name: Consonance and dissonance
concepts.explanation: Consonant combinations sound stable or restful; dissonant ones sound tense and want to move on.
concepts.caveat: What counts as dissonant has changed through history and differs between musical cultures.
concepts.question: Why are dissonant chords essential in music even though they sound tense?

concepts.name: Scale
concepts.explanation: An ordered set of notes used to build melodies and harmonies, such as the major, minor or pentatonic scale.
concepts.caveat: Scales are descriptions of practice, not rules; music often borrows notes from outside them.
concepts.question: Why do so many cultures use pentatonic scales?

concepts.name: Major scale
concepts.explanation: A seven-note scale with the pattern whole-whole-half-whole-whole-whole-half steps, the basis of much Western harmony.
concepts.caveat: Calling major "happy" and minor "sad" is a learned association and an oversimplification.
concepts.question: Which notes of C major are a half step apart?

concepts.name: Key
concepts.explanation: The tonal centre of a piece and the scale built on it; notes and chords are heard in relation to this home note (tonic).
concepts.caveat: Not all music is tonal; atonal and modal music do not have a key in the same sense.
concepts.question: How can you tell which note feels like "home" in a song?

concepts.name: Circle of fifths
concepts.explanation: A diagram arranging keys by perfect fifths, showing how closely related keys share most of their notes.
concepts.caveat: It is a map of relationships for convenience; it does not mean music must move around it.
concepts.question: Why are C major and G major considered closely related keys?

concepts.name: Chord
concepts.explanation: Three or more notes sounded together. Chords are usually built by stacking intervals of a third.
concepts.caveat: Many styles use chords built differently, such as stacked fourths or clusters.
concepts.question: What makes a set of notes a chord rather than just several notes at once?

concepts.name: Triad
concepts.explanation: A three-note chord of root, third and fifth. Its quality (major, minor, diminished, augmented) depends on the intervals.
concepts.caveat: The same triad can sound different depending on which note is in the bass (its inversion).
concepts.question: Which single note changes C major into C minor?

concepts.name: Seventh chord
concepts.explanation: A triad with an added seventh above the root, adding colour and tension; the dominant seventh is central in tonal music.
concepts.caveat: In jazz, sevenths are normal colour rather than tension to be resolved.
concepts.question: Why does G7 pull so strongly toward C?

concepts.name: Chord function
concepts.explanation: The role a chord plays in a key: tonic (stable home), subdominant (moving away) and dominant (tension pulling home).
concepts.caveat: Function depends on context; the same chord can play different roles in different keys or styles.
concepts.question: Why does the V chord feel like it needs to resolve to I?

concepts.name: Chord progression
concepts.explanation: A sequence of chords that gives music a sense of movement and direction, such as I-V-vi-IV.
concepts.caveat: Shared progressions are common across thousands of songs; melody, rhythm and sound make songs distinct.
concepts.question: Why can so many hit songs share the same four chords?

concepts.name: Cadence
concepts.explanation: A chord progression that marks the end of a phrase, like a punctuation mark: authentic (V-I) feels final, half (ending on V) feels open.
concepts.caveat: Cadences are signals within a style; listeners new to a style may not hear them as endings.
concepts.question: Why does ending on the V chord sound like a question?

concepts.name: Voice leading
concepts.explanation: How individual notes move from one chord to the next; smooth voice leading keeps notes close and avoids awkward jumps.
concepts.caveat: Classical voice-leading rules describe one style; breaking them is normal in other styles.
concepts.question: Why do common notes between two chords often stay in the same voice?

concepts.name: Modulation
concepts.explanation: Changing from one key to another within a piece, often using a pivot chord shared by both keys.
concepts.caveat: A brief borrowed chord is not a full modulation; a new key needs to be established.
concepts.question: Why do pop songs often raise the key by a step for the final chorus?
